results.result: Prior work has established that canonical nucleosomes have a well-defined structure (10-nm-wide, 6-nm-thick cylinders with 145-147 bp DNA in 1.65 left-handed superhelical gyres) in vitro, while non-canonical nucleosomes have partially detached DNA, histones, or fewer than eight histones.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 accurately summarize established knowledge from prior crystallography and cryo-EM studies, supported by appropriate citations. These are background claims that set the context for the current work.

results.result: Canonical nucleosomes with GFP tags are abundant in nuclear lysates of H2A-GFP and H2B-GFP strains, with extra densities consistent with GFP positioned according to histone C-terminal locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C71-C77 demonstrate that canonical nucleosomes with visible GFP tags were detected in lysates of LGY0016 (H2A-GFP) and LGY0015 (H2B-GFP) strains at ~25 Å resolution, with GFP densities positioned consistently with known histone C-terminal locations. The data includes 2D and 3D class averages showing nucleosome structural motifs and extra densities.

results.result: Canonical nucleosomes account for less than 10% of expected nucleosomes in wild-type yeast cell cryolamellae, with only ~1500 canonical nucleosomes detected out of ~25,000 expected.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C38-C40, C47, C49-C50, C54, C56, and C108 collectively establish that canonical nucleosomes are rare in situ. The calculation is based on: (1) detection of 769 canonical nucleosomes by VPP imaging and direct 3D classification, (2) accounting for ~50% undersampling of disc views yields ~1500 canonical nucleosomes, and (3) expected ~25,000 total nucleosomes based on published nucleosome numbers and chromatin volume measurements. The <10% estimate is mathematically sound given these values.

results.result: Neither canonical nucleosomes nor nucleosome-like particles with GFP-density protrusions were detected in H2A-GFP strain (LGY0016) cryolamellae in situ.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C80-C82, and C111 demonstrate that despite detecting canonical nucleosomes with GFP tags in LGY0016 lysates, no such structures were found in situ across three different imaging conditions (defocus cryolamellae, VPP cryolamellae, and VPP cryosections). This negative result is well-documented with multiple classification attempts and parameter variations.

results.result: Canonical nucleosomes are rare in budding yeast nuclei in situ, while non-canonical nucleosomes constitute the vast majority, with yeast nucleosomes adopting multiple non-canonical conformations in situ but canonical conformations ex vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84, C123-C125 represent the main conclusion of the study, supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: (1) <10% canonical nucleosomes detected in wild-type cells in situ, (2) abundant canonical nucleosomes in all lysate samples, (3) failure to detect GFP-tagged nucleosomes in situ despite their presence in lysates, and (4) ribosome control experiments confirming technical validity. The model is consistent with all experimental observations.

results.result: The H2A-H2B heterodimer exhibits mobility in situ, remaining attached to the nucleosome but adopting variable orientations, as suggested by the absence of GFP-tagged nucleosome detection in situ and supported by prior structural and biochemical evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C118 propose H2A-H2B mobility as an explanation for the failure to detect GFP-tagged nucleosomes in situ. This interpretation is supported by: (1) the experimental observation that GFP-tagged nucleosomes are visible in lysates but not in situ, (2) prior evidence that ~80% of H2B is chromatin-bound in situ (C115), (3) structural data showing yeast nucleosomes lack stabilizing hydrogen bonds present in metazoan nucleosomes (C116), and (4) recent simulations showing H2A/H2B can adopt multiple orientations while remaining in contact with H3-H4 (C118).

results.result: H3-GFP tagging (without linker, strain LGY0007) enabled detection of GFP-tagged canonical nucleosomes in lysates but not in situ, suggesting that H3-GFP expression makes nucleosomes less ordered in situ.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98, C112, C120-C122 show that only the LGY0007 strain (H3-GFP without linker) produced detectable GFP-tagged nucleosomes in lysates, but no canonical nucleosomes (with or without GFP density) were detected in LGY0007 cryolamellae. This suggests H3-GFP expression perturbs nucleosome structure in situ, though the interpretation is complicated by the fact that even wild-type yeast shows predominantly non-canonical nucleosomes in situ.

results.result: Ribosome subtomogram averaging from cytoplasm achieved ~33 Å resolution (FSC=0.5) from 1,150 particles, with density features consistent with 15-30 Å resolution range, demonstrating that the cryolamellae, data, and workflow are free of pathologies.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 describe a critical control experiment showing that the technical approach is sound. The ribosome resolution (~33 Å) is comparable to recent in situ subtomogram averages using similar particle numbers, and the density features match simulated maps at appropriate resolutions. This validates that the failure to detect canonical nucleosomes in situ is not due to technical limitations.

results.result: The GFP tagging strategy did not work as intended for detecting nucleosomes in situ, and attempts to create sole-source H2B-GFP, H3-GFP, or H4-GFP strains failed, with only H4-GFP viable when using a flexible GGSGGS linker.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C69, C91, C94, and C99 document the limitations and failures of the GFP tagging approach. These negative results are important for understanding the technical challenges and biological constraints of the system. The inability to create sole-source strains for most histones and the failure to detect tagged nucleosomes in situ represent significant experimental outcomes.

results.result: Multiple GFP-tagged yeast strains were successfully constructed and validated, including LGY0016 (H2A-GFP sole source), LGY0015 (H2B-GFP plus wild-type H2B), and several H3-GFP and H4-GFP strains, with genotypes confirmed by PCR, sequencing, immunoblots, and fluorescence microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C68, C70, C92-C93 describe the strain construction and validation methodology. The strains were properly constructed with appropriate genetic modifications, and their genotypes were confirmed by multiple independent methods. The LGY0016 doubling time being ~50% longer than wild-type (C70) indicates the H2A-GFP fusion has biological consequences.

results.result: Cryo-FIB milling is a compression-free method that produces cryolamellae and does not grossly perturb canonical nucleosomes in situ, as evidenced by their detection in HeLa cell cryolamellae.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 establish that cryo-FIB milling is an appropriate sample preparation method. The evidence that canonical nucleosomes were detected in HeLa cells (C30) supports the inference that the method does not grossly perturb nucleosome structure (C31), though this does not rule out subtle effects.

results.result: Multiple classification approaches using defocus phase-contrast imaging of wild-type yeast cryolamellae failed to reveal canonical nucleosome class averages, including the original RELION workflow, direct 3D classification with 100 classes, and biased template matching using the nucleosome crystal structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C37 document systematic attempts to detect canonical nucleosomes using defocus imaging, all yielding negative results. The use of multiple approaches, including an intentionally biased reference (C35), strengthens the conclusion that canonical nucleosomes are rare or absent under these imaging conditions.

results.result: Disc views of canonical nucleosomes are undersampled in situ due to missing hemisphere of views, resulting in roughly half of canonical nucleosomes going undetected.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 identify a systematic bias in the detection method based on angular distribution analysis. This is an important correction factor for estimating the true number of canonical nucleosomes, and the ~50% undersampling estimate is reasonable given the missing disc views. This limitation is properly accounted for in the final calculations (C50, C108).

results.result: High abundance of non-canonical nucleosomes would make more of the genome accessible, consistent with yeast having high levels of transcription, and nucleosome heterogeneity is consistent with the absence of chromatin long-range order in situ.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 draw reasonable biological inferences from the structural findings. The connection between non-canonical nucleosomes and genome accessibility is logical, and the link to absence of long-range chromatin order is supported by the cited literature showing that ordered oligonucleosome arrays require nearly identical sequential nucleosomes.

results.result: Globular complexes as small as canonical nucleosomes (~200 kDa) can be detected by 3D classification of subtomograms from VPP-imaged cryolamellae, but systematic determination of conditions for detecting sub-200 kDa complexes is not yet feasible due to technical limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 accurately assess the current capabilities and limitations of the cryo-ET approach. The detection of ~200 kDa nucleosomes is demonstrated in this work and prior HeLa cell studies, while the limitations for smaller complexes are honestly acknowledged.

results.result: Multiple prior studies using diverse methods (ChIP-seq, MNase-seq, Hi-CO, molecular dynamics simulations, atomic force microscopy, and cryo-EM of nucleosome-protein complexes) have detected non-canonical nucleosomes, nucleosome breathing, DNA unwrapping, and partial DNA detachment in various contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C142 provide extensive literature support for the existence of non-canonical nucleosomes and dynamic nucleosome behavior. These citations appropriately contextualize the current findings within the broader field and show that the observation of non-canonical nucleosomes is consistent with multiple independent lines of evidence from other laboratories and methods.

results.result: Multiple aspects of nucleosome structure in situ remain unknown or uncertain, including the structures of non-canonical nucleosomes, whether one non-canonical structure predominates, the biochemical and biophysical factors responsible for their abundance, and potential effects of GFP tagging.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C10, C18, C85, C109, C119, C128, and C143 honestly acknowledge the limitations and uncertainties of the current work. These statements appropriately identify areas requiring future investigation and potential confounding factors that could not be fully resolved in this study.

results.result: Canonical nucleosomes are abundant in nuclear lysates of wild-type and GFP-tagged yeast strains. The subtomogram averages show canonical nucleosome structures with characteristic 10-nm diameter, 6-nm thick cylindrical shape, left-handed DNA path, and extra linker DNA beyond the 1.65 gyres seen in crystal structures. In H2A-GFP and H2B-GFP strains, extra densities consistent with GFP tags are visible at positions corresponding to the histone C-termini.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the experimental work as 'meticulously performed and convincing' with 'a vast amount of data collected.' The detection of canonical nucleosomes in lysates is not questioned by any reviewer, and the technical quality of the cryo-ET analysis is praised. One reviewer notes the work is 'state-of-the-art' and the authors 'have done everything possible' with current methods.

results.result: Canonical nucleosomes are rare in wild-type yeast cell cryolamellae. Using VPP imaging and direct 3D classification, only ~769 canonical nucleosomes were detected (estimated ~1500 accounting for undersampling), representing less than 10% of the expected ~25,000 total nucleosomes in the sampled nuclear volume. This suggests that >90% of yeast nucleosomes in situ are non-canonical.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the experimental rigor ('meticulously performed'), one reviewer explicitly states 'I am not ready to agree with their conclusion that heterogenous non-canonical nucleosomes predominate in yeast cells' and notes 'it is hard to prove that something is not there.' Another reviewer questions whether 'the yeast nucleoplasm is differently structured than that of HeLa cells' making nucleosomes harder to find by template matching. The controversial nature is acknowledged by editors who note the work 'will spark thought-provoking debate.'

results.result: Neither canonical nucleosomes nor nucleosome-like particles with GFP-tag densities were detected in H2A-GFP (LGY0016) or H3-GFP (LGY0007) strain cryolamellae. The 3D class averages show structures that do not resemble canonical nucleosomes, even though some have DNA-like motifs that do not wrap 1.65 times around the center as expected.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these negative findings as part of the comprehensive experimental approach. One reviewer notes the authors 'have done everything possible to test that hypothesis with today's available methods' and commends 'the massive amount of work.' The absence of expected GFP-tagged structures is treated as a significant finding rather than a technical failure.

results.result: The authors conclude that canonical nucleosomes are rare in budding yeast nuclei in situ, non-canonical nucleosomes are the vast majority, and the yeast intracellular environment disfavors the canonical nucleosome conformation. The data support a model where yeast nucleosomes are abundant and canonical ex vivo but adopt multiple non-canonical conformations in situ.
results.evaluation: This central conclusion receives mixed evaluation. One reviewer explicitly states reluctance to agree ('I am not ready to agree with their conclusion'), while another finds it 'consistent with the unstable property of yeast nucleosomes and the high proportion of the actively transcribed yeast genome.' The editors acknowledge the 'possibly controversial nature of this report' and note it 'will spark thought-provoking debate,' indicating the field needs to 'carefully evaluate the data and assess whether the claims are supported.'

results.result: The absence of GFP-tagged nucleosome structures in situ suggests H2A-H2B heterodimer mobility, meaning the heterodimer remains attached but can adopt different orientations. This interpretation is supported by crystallographic evidence that yeast nucleosomes lack stabilizing hydrogen bonds present in metazoan nucleosomes, exposure of H2A-H2B/H3 interfaces to small molecules, and simulations showing the heterodimer can adopt numerous orientations while remaining in contact with H3-H4.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation as consistent with the data. One reviewer notes the authors 'stumble over new insights into nucleosome arrangement that indicates that the positions of the histones is more flexible than previously believed.' The mechanistic explanation drawing on crystallographic and simulation data is not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: As a technical control, subtomogram averaging of cytoplasmic ribosomes achieved ~33 Å resolution (FSC=0.5) from 1,150 particles, with density features consistent with 15-30 Å resolution range. This resolution is comparable to recent in situ subtomogram averages and demonstrates that the cryolamellae, data, and workflow do not show evidence of pathologies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question this control experiment. The technical quality is implicitly accepted as part of the overall assessment that the work is 'meticulously performed' with 'state-of-the-art nature of the technology.' No concerns are raised about the ribosome control validating the methodology.

results.result: The GFP-tagging strategy had limitations: tagged nucleosome 3D classes could not be detected in situ for H2A-GFP, and strains with H2B-GFP, H3-GFP, or H4-GFP as sole sources could not be created (except H2A-GFP). The authors conclude that H2A-H2B properties make this pair a poor candidate for GFP fusion, and H3/H4-GFP fusions cannot be used to detect non-canonical nucleosomes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these methodological limitations as honestly reported. One reviewer notes the authors 'have done a really great job with including all their results to the benefit of the scientific community,' implicitly praising the transparent reporting of what did not work. The extensive efforts with multiple tagging strategies are acknowledged.

results.result: The high abundance of non-canonical nucleosomes would make more of the genome accessible, consistent with yeast having high transcription levels. Nucleosome heterogeneity is also consistent with the absence of chromatin long-range order in situ, since crystalline oligonucleosome arrays require sequential nucleosomes to adopt nearly identical conformations.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly notes the finding is 'consistent with the unstable property of yeast nucleosomes and the high proportion of the actively transcribed yeast genome.' The biological interpretation connecting structural heterogeneity to functional properties is accepted as reasonable by reviewers who find the work 'informative to the chromatin/chromosome field.'

results.result: The study demonstrates that globular complexes as small as canonical nucleosomes (~200 kDa) can be detected by 3D classification of subtomograms from VPP-imaged cryolamellae. However, it is not yet feasible to systematically determine conditions for detecting sub-200 kDa complexes given current technical limitations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as an important technical advance. The editors note the work 'exploits new cryo-EM tomography tools' and reviewers state 'these kinds of tools represent an important advance for in situ analysis of chromatin.' The technical limitations are acknowledged as realistic given current technology.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the main conclusion (C83-C84, C123-C125) that non-canonical nucleosomes predominate in yeast. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED by convergent evidence, while peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN - one explicitly states reluctance to agree, and editors acknowledge the controversial nature requiring field debate.

Both evaluate the ribosome control experiment (C86-C89). Both find this SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes it validates technical soundness, peer reviewers implicitly accept it as part of 'meticulously performed' work without raising concerns.

Both evaluate biological inferences about genome accessibility and chromatin order (C126-C127). Both find this SUPPORTED - OpenEval calls the connections 'reasonable,' peer reviewers note consistency with 'unstable property of yeast nucleosomes and high proportion of actively transcribed genome.'

Both evaluate technical capabilities and limitations (C129-C130). Both find this SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes honest acknowledgment of limitations, peer reviewers accept this as 'important technical advance' with realistic limitations given current technology.

Both evaluate H2A-H2B mobility explanation (C113-C118, with peer also including C122). Both find this SUPPORTED - OpenEval cites structural and simulation evidence, peer reviewers note authors 'stumble over new insights' about histone flexibility without challenging the interpretation.

Both address rarity of canonical nucleosomes in situ (C22, C38-C40, C47, C49-C50, C54, C56, C108, with peer also including C33-C35, C37, C107). OpenEval finds the <10% calculation SUPPORTED and mathematically sound. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN - acknowledging experimental rigor but questioning the conclusion, noting 'it is hard to prove that something is not there' and questioning whether yeast nucleoplasm structure affects detection.

Both evaluate GFP tagging limitations and failures (C59, C69, C91, C99, with peer also including C90). Both find this SUPPORTED - OpenEval notes these negative results are important for understanding constraints, peer reviewers praise transparent reporting and note authors 'have done a really great job with including all their results.'

Both evaluate detection of canonical nucleosomes in lysates (C21, C25, C71-C77, with peer also including C96, C97, C106). Both find this SUPPORTED - OpenEval confirms GFP-tagged nucleosomes detected at ~25Å resolution, peer reviewers call work 'meticulously performed and convincing' with technical quality praised as 'state-of-the-art.'

Both evaluate failure to detect GFP-tagged nucleosomes in situ (C23, C80-C82, C111, with peer also including C112, C120-C121). Both find this SUPPORTED - OpenEval documents systematic negative results across imaging conditions, peer reviewers accept these as significant findings rather than technical failures, noting 'massive amount of work.'

OpenEval R12 evaluates systematic defocus imaging attempts (C33-C35, C37) finding them SUPPORTED. These claims overlap with peer R2's broader evaluation of canonical nucleosome rarity, where peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY about the overall conclusion despite acknowledging experimental rigor.

OpenEval R7 addresses H3-GFP strain perturbations (C97-C98, C112, C120-C122) finding evidence SUPPORTED. Peer R3 includes some overlapping claims (C112, C120-C121) as part of broader GFP tagging failures, which they find SUPPORTED as honest negative results.

OpenEval evaluates background claims from prior crystallography and cryo-EM studies (C1-C5) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - these are contextual claims not specifically addressed by reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates strain construction and validation methodology (C61-C68, C70, C92-C93) as SUPPORTED, noting proper genetic modifications and biological consequences. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - reviewers did not specifically comment on strain construction details.

OpenEval evaluates cryo-FIB milling methodology (C28-C31) as SUPPORTED, noting detection in HeLa cells validates the approach. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - reviewers did not specifically address sample preparation method validation.

OpenEval evaluates angular distribution bias and undersampling correction (C45-C46) as SUPPORTED, noting ~50% undersampling is properly accounted for in calculations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - reviewers did not specifically address this technical correction factor.

OpenEval evaluates extensive literature support for non-canonical nucleosomes (C132-C142) as SUPPORTED, noting appropriate contextualization within broader field. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - reviewers did not specifically evaluate the literature citations.

OpenEval evaluates acknowledgment of limitations and uncertainties (C6, C10, C18, C85, C109, C119, C128, C143) as SUPPORTED, praising honest identification of areas requiring future work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found as a distinct result, though peer reviewers generally praised transparent reporting throughout.
